glance: OpenAI has broken up its dedicated robotics team, betting that its general model can control robots directly, and Cursor has traced its poisoned Claude Code extension to a leaked key at inference provider Fireworks AI. Also: a four-hour US flight stop puts an AI routing tool under scrutiny, llama.cpp reaches version 1.0, Hexagon completes its Waygate deal, and recalls at Toyota and Honda. Two new papers cover physics-informed ultrasonic inspection and cavitation in engine main bearings.
brief: OpenAI has disbanded its standalone robotics team. OpenAI now believes its general model, GPT-6 Astra, can control robots directly. In one simulated test it beat the best specialised robot models, seventy-five percent to fifty-one, though it still fails most hard real-world tasks. Cursor has explained how tampered versions of the Claude Code extension reached its marketplace last month. A key held by its inference provider, Fireworks AI, exposed agent logs that contained credentials, which the attacker used to get in. Up to five thousand users may have received the backdoored versions. In the United States, the aviation regulator halted all flights for more than four hours. The maker of its new AI routing tool says the tool was not the cause, and officials see no sign of a cyberattack. The local AI engine llama.cpp reached version one point zero, with a stable interface for apps. Replit's agent can now make purchases and run Google ad campaigns, with a person approving any spending. Corsair joined the Ansys partner programme with GPU machines for simulation, and Hexagon completed its takeover of the inspection company Waygate. Toyota is recalling about sixty-two thousand Tundras over faulty camshafts, and Honda more than six hundred thousand cars over steering software. MAN signed an electric truck rental deal, Strabag bought into German motorway truck charging, Audi set up a parts reuse company, and Xpeng plans a big push into the UK. In research, a physics-informed network speeds up ultrasonic defect scans, and a simulation study shows how groove geometry cuts cavitation in engine bearings.

stories.headline: OpenAI disbands its standalone robotics team, betting general models can run robots
stories.why: If one general model can drive both software agents and physical machines, robotics and factory automation stop being a separate AI stack.
body: OpenAI has broken up its dedicated robotics team, according to a Fortune exclusive published on Friday and followed up by The Decoder on Saturday. Robotics researchers move into the main research group under chief research officer Mark Chen, while the applied robotics and hardware staff join Greg Brockman's Applied organisation. The change was abrupt enough that OpenAI's booth at the CoRL robotics conference in Austin was left empty.

The reasoning is that OpenAI now thinks its general model, GPT-6 Astra, can control robots directly. In an Nvidia study cited by Fortune, an Astra-powered agent scored 74.8% on a simulated manipulation benchmark, against 51.0% for the best specialised robot models. On a harder benchmark it fully completed only 7 of 100 tasks, so the gap to reliable real-world use is still large. It is the second time OpenAI has shut robotics: it closed the team in 2020 and rebuilt it in 2024. The company says robotics remains core to its long-term plans and still aims for a humanoid demo in 2027.
For manufacturing and test engineers, the bet matters because it suggests robot programming may move towards prompting large general models rather than training task-specific controllers.

stories.headline: Cursor traces its poisoned Claude Code extension to a leaked key at Fireworks AI
stories.why: A second AI product has now been hit through the same inference vendor, so teams need to audit what their model providers can reach.
body: Cursor has published the root cause of the incident in late October, when tampered versions of the Claude Code extension appeared in its marketplace. A key that Cursor had issued to Fireworks AI, the company that hosted some of its open-weight inference, was exposed. It gave read-only access to a shared storage bucket of coding-agent traces, mostly from 2025 sessions run outside Privacy Mode. Some of those traces contained credentials, which the attacker then used to get into Cursor's own services.

On 29 October a stolen credential let the attacker plant versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 of the extension in Cursor's marketplace cache for about 11 hours, reaching up to 5,000 users. The backdoor tried to add an SSH key, open a reverse tunnel and send out secrets from environment variables. Cursor says fewer than 0.05% of users had traces exposed, Privacy Mode prompts and customer code were not affected, and the last attacker activity was on 1 November.

Cursor has moved inference off Fireworks, revoked vendor access and rebuilt its marketplace. Notion reported a breach through the same provider earlier this week. The lesson for product teams is to keep secrets out of agent sessions and treat logged traces as sensitive data.

stories.headline: FAA halts all US flights for four hours; maker of its new AI routing tool says it was not to blame
stories.why: It shows how quickly suspicion falls on new AI systems when old infrastructure fails, a pattern any team rolling out AI in operations will face.
body: The US Federal Aviation Administration ordered a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday that lasted more than four hours, citing an equipment outage. Thousands of flights were cancelled, Chicago O'Hare alone logged 208 cancellations by early evening, and Mexico put temporary restrictions on flights to the US. Recovery continued through Saturday.

Attention quickly turned to SMART, an AI tool for rerouting air traffic that the FAA extended to all 22 US air traffic centres on 10 November. AirSpace Intel, the contractor behind it, said neither SMART nor its integrations caused the stop. Homeland security officials and the FAA said there was no sign of a cyberattack, though the investigation continues. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed old, overloaded technology and asked Congress for billions more in funding. One outlet reports that contractors cut legacy copper lines during a fibre installation, but this has not been confirmed officially.
The episode is a reminder that AI added on top of ageing systems gets judged by the reliability of the whole chain, not just the model.

stories.headline: llama.cpp and ggml reach version 1.0 with a stable programming interface
stories.why: The most widely used engine for running models locally now promises not to break apps between minor releases, which makes on-device AI easier to ship.
body: The open-source projects llama.cpp and ggml, which power much of the local and on-device AI ecosystem, released version 1.0.0 on Friday, about three and a half years after launch. Both now follow semantic versioning: any breaking change to the C programming interface or binary interface will require a new major version.

The 1.0 release removes deprecated functions, so apps that embed the library need to check for those when they upgrade. The engine supports more than 150 model architecture variants and the common speculative-decoding methods, and it builds for Linux, macOS, Windows, Android and iOS. It is packaged for Docker, Homebrew, Debian, conda-forge and Winget, and Nvidia, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel contribute hardware test machines.

For product teams, a stable interface lowers the maintenance cost of features that run models on laptops, phones or edge devices instead of in the cloud. That helps with privacy-sensitive features and offline use, and it makes local inference a more realistic option for desktop and mobile apps.

stories.headline: Replit's agent can now buy things and run Google Ads campaigns, with a human approving spend
stories.why: App-building tools are moving from making software to operating the business around it, and the approval step is the design pattern to copy.
body: Replit has given its coding agent two new powers. With agentic commerce, built on Stripe's Link and Visa, the agent can make one-time purchases for US users on Core and Pro plans. It prepares checkout in an isolated browser and stops for the owner to approve the final total, and shell access and general browsing are switched off during payment.

With Agentic Ads, available to Pro users worldwide, the agent drafts ad copy and images, suggests daily budgets and sets up conversion tracking across Google Search, YouTube, Display and Discover. Nothing is spent until a person approves. Users can connect an existing Google Ads account or fund a Replit-managed one from their Replit credits. Replit says the number of builders connecting Stripe has grown ninefold since May. It has not published pricing or spending caps.

For product managers, the release shows how agent features are being packaged: narrow, high-value actions, a sandboxed execution environment and an explicit confirmation step at the moment money moves.

stories.headline: Corsair joins the Ansys partner programme with GPU workstations and servers sized for simulation
stories.why: More vendors are tuning hardware for GPU-based CFD and FEA, which changes how test and simulation departments budget compute.
body: Corsair has joined the Ansys Technology Partner Program, now run by Synopsys, with its CORSAIR PRO line of workstations, servers and clusters. The company says it will build configurations matched to the Ansys application, model size, licensing and budget of each customer.

The FlexPrime workstations are aimed at pre- and post-processing and single-node studies, with the top model claimed at over 400 teraflops in single precision. FlexGrid GPU servers target multi-GPU Fluent runs and on-premises use of SimAI, Ansys's AI surrogate tool, with nearly 500 teraflops in double precision claimed. Clusters cover distributed CPU solves. These are vendor figures.

At the SC26 supercomputing conference in Chicago from 15 to 20 November, Corsair will show Fluent results streamed into Nvidia Omniverse, and Synopsys will present GPU-accelerated Fluent benchmarks on Nvidia Blackwell. For automotive CAE teams, the practical question is whether on-premises GPU machines now beat cloud or CPU clusters on cost per simulation for CFD and AI surrogates.

stories.headline: Hexagon completes its takeover of Waygate Technologies, joining metrology and NDT
stories.why: One supplier can now cover CT, ultrasonic testing and coordinate measurement, which may simplify inspection set-ups in bearing and drivetrain plants.
body: Hexagon has closed its acquisition of Waygate Technologies from Baker Hughes, about seven months after the deal was announced in April. Closing was reported on 3 November and wider trade coverage followed this week. Waygate becomes part of Hexagon's Manufacturing Intelligence division.

Waygate brings industrial computed tomography, field radiography, ultrasonic testing and remote visual inspection. Hexagon adds coordinate measuring machines, portable measuring arms, scanners and metrology software. Michael Bellamy stays on as Waygate's chief executive, and Hexagon says existing projects, service agreements and orders continue without interruption. Neither company has given a deal value or headcount in the coverage.

For manufacturers of bearing rings, gears and shafts, the combination points towards inspection lines where CT and ultrasonic defect data sit in the same software as dimensional measurement. That could make it easier to link internal defects to geometry and to feed both into quality analytics and AI-based defect detection.

stories.headline: Toyota recalls 62,000 Tundras over camshafts from one bad supplier lot; Honda recalls 635,808 cars over steering software
stories.why: Two recalls in one week show that both supplier lot traceability and software fail-safe behaviour are now central quality risks.
body: Toyota is recalling about 62,000 non-hybrid Tundra pickups in the US from model years 2022–23 and 2025–26. Around 300 camshafts from a single supplier production lot are suspect, and a broken camshaft can cause loss of power at higher speed. Every truck in the recall will be inspected and affected camshafts replaced free of charge, with owners notified by mid-January 2027. It follows a 2024 recall of the same twin-turbo V6 over machining debris.
In the same week's NHTSA listings, Honda and Acura are recalling 635,808 vehicles because the electric power steering software can enter a fail-safe mode that removes steering assist.

Together they illustrate two sides of modern vehicle quality. On the hardware side, recall size is driven by how precisely a supplier lot can be traced to individual vehicles. On the software side, a fail-safe that works as designed can still create a hazard for the driver, which puts more weight on testing how degraded modes feel in real driving.

stories.headline: MAN signs a rental deal for electric trucks with Hylane as Strabag buys into Autobahn truck charging
stories.why: Electric heavy trucks are moving into pay-per-use fleets, and the charging network they need is being built and financed now.
body: Truck rental firm Hylane of Cologne has signed a long-term framework agreement with MAN, starting with 20 eTGX electric tractors. Customers rent them pay-per-use, billed monthly per kilometre, on contracts from 24 to 108 months. The trucks carry up to 480 kWh of usable battery, are rated for up to 570 km and charge at up to 375 kW, with optional megawatt charging up to 750 kW. Using the EU's extra two-tonne allowance for zero-emission trucks, the partners say payload matches a diesel at about 25 tonnes. Hylane began with hydrogen trucks in 2021 and added battery-electric ones in 2025.

Separately, construction group Strabag has bought 50% of charging operator R:loaded. Its consortium won one lot of Germany's national Autobahn truck fast-charging network: 140 charging points at 25 unstaffed rest areas in southern and western Germany, which R:loaded will run until mid-2034. The price was not disclosed.
For drivetrain and bearing engineers, rental duty cycles with high mileage and frequent fast charging are a useful stress case for e-axle durability.

stories.headline: Audi sets up a company to sell used genuine parts and recover materials from end-of-life cars
stories.why: The EU's planned end-of-life vehicle rules are turning recycled content and parts reuse into an engineering requirement, not just a sustainability goal.
body: Audi is launching Audi Circular Solutions, a wholly owned subsidiary that starts work in early 2027. Its first job is a central sales channel for used genuine Audi parts in Germany and other European markets, with other brands to follow later.

Later phases will add buying used vehicles and components, managing dismantling partners and securing secondary raw materials, with recycled plastics the first priority. It will begin by dismantling cars Audi already owns, such as its internal fleet, and builds on Audi's MaterialLoop pilots and the Volkswagen Group's dismantling line in Zwickau. Michael Gick is managing director. No volume or revenue targets were given.

The trigger is the EU's planned End-of-Life Vehicles Regulation, which would require a minimum share of recycled plastic in new cars. For development teams, that means material specifications, validation of recycled grades and design for disassembly will need to be considered earlier. For suppliers, reused parts raise new questions about remaining life and requalification testing.

stories.headline: Xpeng plans five right-hand-drive models and about 100 UK sites to lead the premium EV market by 2028
stories.why: Chinese brands are now targeting the premium segment in Europe with driver assistance as a selling point, not just low prices.
body: Chinese carmaker Xpeng says it wants to lead the UK premium electric car market by 2028. It plans five right-hand-drive models within 12 months, starting with the L03 and G9L, each offered as a battery-electric car and as a Kunpeng extended-range version with a small combustion engine acting as a generator.

The company plans about 100 retail and service sites during 2027, three flagship stores in London and Manchester within six months and around 20 dealer and leasing partners. A national parts hub is meant to supply stores within 24 hours. Its NGP driver assistance system, built on its VLA 2.0 model, is planned for the UK in 2027, and Google Play integration is due early that year.

Reaching the goal would mean overtaking BMW and Tesla in UK premium within two years. For European OEMs and suppliers, the plan shows extended-range drivetrains and AI-based driver assistance becoming key competitive features in a market with no EU tariffs on Chinese cars.

stories.headline: Physics-informed neural network separates defect echoes from ultrasonic guided waves and cuts scan points by seven times
stories.why: Physics-based models of the healthy part could make ultrasonic inspection faster and easier to trust than purely data-driven defect detectors.
body: Researchers at the German Aerospace Center's Institute of Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul and RWTH Aachen University have posted a preprint, now under peer review, on finding damage with ultrasonic guided waves. They train a neural network with sine-based activations to obey the wave equations of a thin plate, so it acts as a model of the undamaged part. Subtracting that model from the measured wavefield leaves the waves scattered by a defect. A coarse scan then finds the defect and an adaptive scan refines it.

In tests on 3 mm aluminium plates, the full method reconstructed the wavefield with about 79% lower error than a data-only network and located simulated defects with a median error of 0.45 mm. On real measurements it found a milled notch within 2.63 mm. The adaptive scan needed about one seventh of the points of a dense scan, and inference takes under a millisecond.
The work covers flat plates only, but the idea of subtracting a physics model of the healthy part could carry over to inspecting rings, shafts and gears, where scan time and explainability matter.

stories.headline: Simulation shows a larger fillet radius cuts cavitation by two thirds where oil groove meets oil hole in a diesel main bearing
stories.why: Small changes to drilling and groove geometry are a cheap way to reduce cavitation erosion in engine and driveline plain bearings.
body: A peer-reviewed paper in Lubricants from China's National Key Laboratory of Marine Engine Science and Technology in Shanghai and the Naval University of Engineering in Wuhan looks at cavitation where the oil groove meets the oil hole in a diesel engine main bearing. The team used large eddy simulation with a multiphase cavitation model and varied four geometry features: fillet radius, chamfer angle, groove depth and the shape of the groove end. Cavitation was tracked separately on the bearing shell and on the journal side.

Raising the fillet radius from 3 to 5 mm cut time-integrated cavitation by about 66% on the shell side and 23% on the journal side. A 30-degree chamfer also helped, while a deeper groove made cavitation worse on both sides. Smooth curved groove ends lowered peak velocity but produced jets that clung to the wall, so cavitation lasted longer overall.
The study is simulation only, with no experimental validation reported, so it is best read as a guide for which geometry changes to test on a rig first.

watch.title: Nvidia results and leadership
watch.text: Nvidia reports quarterly results on 17 November, its first under interim CEO Colette Kress, with new board chair Harvey Jones in place.

watch.title: Tesla driver assistance in the EU
watch.text: Eleven countries now accept the Dutch approval of Tesla's supervised system, but an EU-wide vote in the technical committee on motor vehicles has no date yet.

watch.title: EU rules for AI shopping agents
watch.text: The Commission's proposed Digital Fairness Act would require users to set how much an AI purchasing agent can buy without approval. It now goes to Parliament and Council.
